Ascriptions of moral responsibility fundamentally presuppose that agents possess a genuine counterfactual competence, meaning they could have done otherwise under the exact same circumstances. In a purely causal-mechanical universe, however, every event is the inevitable consequence of antecedent physical states and immutable natural laws, leaving no room for alternative possibilities. To assert that an agent could have acted differently within such a deterministic framework requires the introduction of concepts like choice, deliberation, and rational evaluation. This introduction represents a normative surplus—an injection of evaluative and agentic concepts that are entirely absent from, and cannot be derived from, the vocabulary of particles, forces, and physical trajectories. A purely mechanistic description can only account for what is, whereas the counterfactual competence required for moral responsibility demands an account of what ought to have been or what could have been in a morally significant sense. Consequently, the physicalist framework cannot satisfy this counterfactual requirement without illegitimately smuggling in the very normative agency it seeks to reduce or deny, demonstrating that moral responsibility cannot be grounded in purely mechanical causal chains.

This necessity of a non-reducible conception of agency becomes even more apparent when examining the reactive attitudes that constitute the core of human moral practices. Emotions such as resentment, indignation, and gratitude are not merely visceral, non-rational reactions to pleasant or unpleasant stimuli; rather, they are complex, cognitively rich attitudes that are intelligible only when directed at entities perceived as genuine sources of reasons-responsive action. When we feel resentment toward someone who has harmed us, we are not merely reacting to a physical cause, as we might toward a falling branch or a malfunctioning machine. Instead, we are holding them accountable for a failure of moral regard, a stance that presupposes the agent acted on, or failed to act on, reasons that they were capable of recognizing and evaluating. To treat a human being merely as a node in a causal network—where actions are the inevitable output of neurological and environmental inputs—is to adopt an objective attitude that bypasses moral engagement entirely and views the individual as an object to be managed, trained, or avoided. The very intelligibility of our moral lives thus depends on viewing agents as active evaluators of reasons, a status that is conceptually incompatible with a reductionist framework that collapses agency into mere physical causation.

Faced with the tension between determinism and moral practice, compatibilist attempts to reconstruct agency within a deterministic framework succeed only by executing a conceptual sleight of hand that shifts the target of inquiry. These accounts typically attempt to salvage the requirement that an agent could have done otherwise by redefining this capacity in conditional or dispositional terms, suggesting that to say an agent could have acted differently is merely to say that they would have acted differently if their desires, beliefs, or motivations had been different. While this maneuver successfully preserves the linguistic form of responsibility attribution, it completely abandons its normative substance. By translating a robust, categorical capacity for alternative action into a mere conditional disposition, compatibilism reduces the agent to a highly complex, self-regulating mechanism whose choices are still ultimately dictated by antecedent conditions beyond their control. This dispositional redefinition fails to capture the moral intuition that an agent is truly blameworthy only if, given the exact state of the universe at the moment of decision, they possessed the active power to choose a different path. Consequently, compatibilist reconstructions of agency offer only a hollow imitation of responsibility, proving that any attempt to ground moral accountability within a purely causal-mechanical framework must inevitably sacrifice the very normative core it seeks to defend.
